stances.claim: CJ has long admired George Erwin Garcia as an election lawyer of competence, integrity, and dignity -- and cheered his Comelec ascension -- but Garcia has now led the Comelec into 'not just simple errors but grave abuse of discretion (GAD),' which requires more than mere abuse but gravely abusive or whimsical and arbitrary conduct.

In Smartmatic v Comelec (April 16, 2024, J Marquez, en banc, 15-0), the SC reversed the Comelec's disqualification of Smartmatic based merely on US DOJ information about ex-Chair Bautista's 2016 procurement -- a violation of Comelec's own rules and Smartmatic's due-process rights -- and CJ supports this even though he does not favor Smartmatic, because due process and the rule of law must always be observed.
The Court applied the operative-fact doctrine prospectively to preserve the Comelec's Miru-Systems award and avoid 2025-election infeasibility, while lecturing Comelec on proper procedures.

In De Guzman-Lara v Comelec (Aug 6, 2024, J Lopez, en banc, 13-0-2), the Court ruled that a day has 24 hours and that a petition filed by email beyond office hours but before midnight is timely; 'institutions with vast innovative resources such as the Comelec' should be able to access pleadings filed via email.

In Macalintal v Comelec, the Court en banc issued an ex parte TRO against Comelec's resolution allowing appointive party-list nominees to remain in office until automatic resignation at the start of the campaign period -- a two-month head-start during which public officials could use government resources to promote their party-list, an abhorrent practice already thrashed in Quinto v Comelec (Feb 22, 2010, CJ Puno, en banc) holding that appointive officials are deemed resigned upon COC filing.

Garcia's two recent administrative leads -- calling for an amendment to the party-list law (the SC having 'opened the flood gates to the dynasts, the powerful and the rich') and publishing all COCs on Comelec's website for public scrutiny -- are agreeable.

Despite the agreement on administrative leads, CJ still asks 'quo vadis, Chair Garcia,' hoping Garcia will redeem himself in quasi-judicial matters by sticking to his election-law expertise -- one GAD chastisement may be acceptable, but multiple are painful for a lawyer of his caliber and stature.

notable_anecdotes: CJ's opening admission -- 'I cheered his ascension as chair' -- turning the column into a memoir of disappointment by an earlier supporter, not an attack by a critic.

The non-partisan due-process credential -- 'I do not favor Smartmatic in any way, except that I believe that due process and the rule of law must always be observed in our democracy' -- modeling CJ's principled independence even when defending a controversial vendor.
The De Guzman-Lara teaching detail -- 'a day is composed of 24 hours' -- quoted as if the SC were having to remind the Comelec of an elementary fact, a quiet judicial-sarcasm preservation.
The 'institutions with vast innovative resources such as the Comelec' SC quotation -- a teaching moment about email accessibility, included as gentle institutional reproof.

The Quinto v Comelec confrontation -- pointedly authored by 'CJ Reynato S. Puno, en banc' -- used as the prior-precedent baseline that the Macalintal-challenged Comelec resolution defied, with CJ adding that 'as a seasoned election lawyer, Garcia should have known the evil.'

The closing arithmetic -- 'One chastisement for committing GAD may be acceptable, but multiple times? Quite painful for a lawyer of his caliber and stature' -- turning a rhetorical question into a quantified professional reproof.
The 'In the next case, I hope to cheer his rise' close -- explicitly preserving the door for vindication, which the sequel A154 (Oct 28) will track as having further narrowed.

one_paragraph_summary: CJ has long admired George Erwin Garcia as an election lawyer of competence, integrity, and dignity -- and cheered his ascension as Comelec chair -- but Garcia has now led the Comelec into 'not just simple errors but grave abuse of discretion (GAD)' multiple times. In Smartmatic v Comelec (April 16, 2024, J Marquez, en banc, 15-0), the Court reversed the Comelec for disqualifying Smartmatic based merely on US DOJ information about an ongoing criminal investigation into former Comelec Chair Juan Andres D. Bautista -- a violation of Comelec's own rules and Smartmatic's due-process rights. CJ does not favor Smartmatic in any way, but believes 'due process and the rule of law must always be observed in our democracy.' The Court applied the operative-fact doctrine prospectively to preserve the Comelec's Miru-Systems award and avoid 2025-election infeasibility, while lecturing Comelec on proper future procedure. In De Guzman-Lara v Comelec (Aug 6, 2024, J Lopez, en banc, 13-0-2), the Court taught the poll body that 'a day is composed of 24 hours' and that an email petition received before midnight is timely -- 'institutions with vast innovative resources such as the Comelec' should be able to access pleadings filed beyond office hours. In Macalintal v Comelec, the Court issued an ex parte TRO against Comelec's resolution allowing public appointive party-list nominees to remain in office for about two months until automatic resignation at the start of the campaign period -- an abhorrent practice already thrashed in Quinto v Comelec (Feb 22, 2010, CJ Puno, en banc) holding that all appointive officials are deemed resigned upon COC filing, which 'as a seasoned election lawyer, Garcia should have known.' CJ agrees with Garcia's two recent administrative leads -- calling for an amendment to the party-list law (the SC having 'opened the flood gates to the dynasts, the powerful and the rich') and publishing all COCs online for public scrutiny -- but still asks 'quo vadis, Chair Garcia,' hoping he will redeem himself in quasi-judicial matters by sticking to his election-law expertise. 'One chastisement for committing GAD may be acceptable, but multiple times? Quite painful for a lawyer of his caliber and stature. In the next case, I hope to cheer his rise.'
